system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 30 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Mission: Search freely for the most promising selective dependencies in the data.

Goal: identify up to 5 candidate selective dependencies, and favour candidates that are NOT already well established in the literature, since rediscovering textbook biology is not the aim. Pre-register, replicate, and submit honest findings, including failures.

input.summary: None of the 5 registered hypotheses replicated. The strongest genome-wide signals in the discovery data came mostly from passenger "LOSS_" markers that stood in for haematopoietic subtypes, mainly mature B-cell neoplasms. Lineage adjustment did not remove this because the subtype sits inside the Lymphoid lineage. I chose candidates that weren't textbook biology, but each one rested on a subtype-proxy biomarker or on very few altered lines (n=7–14). Classic positive controls did not appear in the discovery scans I ran: LOSS_MTAP→PRMT5 was missing from LOSS_MTAP's top hits, and MUT_SMARCA4→SMARCA2 was missing in both directions. That is a reason to doubt this data's resolution, not a known artefact. The Python sandbox failed to load data, so I could not run custom paralog-pair screens. In held-out lines all five effects shrank sharply. H5 (ENKD1 loss→HRAS) gave a strong Sanger signal from only 3 altered lines, but the held-out Broad result was weak (p=0.054), so it did not pass. Lesson: in this data, top lineage-adjusted hits with heme-subtype-enriched biomarkers and n<30 are mostly overfit. Future searches should adjust for disease subtype and use biomarkers with a direct mechanistic link to the target.

findings.claim: MARCKS-silenced (mostly haematopoietic) lines were more NMNAT1-dependent in discovery data (t=-6.6), but the lineage-adjusted effect vanished in held-out Broad (p=0.24) and Sanger (p=0.44) lines.
SYNJ2 loss (a proxy for B-cell neoplasms) predicted HERPUD1 dependency in discovery data, but not in held-out Broad (p=0.086) or Sanger (p=0.94) lines.
PON2-lost heme lines looked PEDS1 (plasmalogen) dependent in discovery data; there was only weak support in Sanger (p=0.035) and none in held-out Broad lines (p=0.32).
The link between damaging TRRAP mutation and KIDINS220 dependency (n=8) did not replicate (p=0.17 held-out, p=0.16 Sanger); it is likely a small-n false positive.

ENKD1-silenced mesenchymal lines (mesothelioma, sarcoma, rhabdoid) were more HRAS-dependent in discovery and Sanger data (Sanger p=9e-8, only 3 altered lines), but the held-out Broad result missed the threshold (p=0.054), so it failed the pre-registered criterion.

In held-out lines all five effects shrank sharply. H5 (ENKD1 loss→HRAS) gave a strong Sanger signal from only 3 altered lines, but the held-out Broad result was weak (p=0.054), so it did not pass. Lesson: in this data, top lineage-adjusted hits with heme-subtype-enriched biomarkers and n<30 are mostly overfit. Future searches should adjust for disease subtype and use biomarkers with a direct mechanistic link to the target.
